To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the maternal serum concentrations of PlGF and sFlt‐1 in combination with maternal and fetal factors at 19–20 weeks' gestation can identify SGA neonates with 80% sensitivity and 75% specificity and can predict delivery at <32 weeks with a positive predictive value (PPV) of 40% (95% CI: 30–50%) and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 95% (95% 91–98%).

the maternal serum concentration of PlGF and sFlt‐1, in combination with the maternal factors and fetal ultrasound biometry at 19–20 weeks, are useful in the prediction of the delivery of SGA neonates, in women without PE, and that such assessment may be helpful in deciding whether a third‐trimesterscan should be performed at either 32 and/or at 36 weeks of gestation.

the maternal serum concentrations of sFlt‐1 and PAPP‐A at 19–20 weeks of gestation in combination with maternal characteristics (age, height, ethnicity) and fetal abdominal circumference (AC) at the same scan are predictive of SGA neonates in the absence of PE.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new and more accurate methods for the prediction of SGA, and the use of this information in the management of pregnancy.
the prediction of small‐for­‐gestational‐­age (SGA).
the prediction of small‐for gestational age (SGA) at birth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of a screening test for SGA in the absence of PE is not justified, and should not be recommended.

the use of maternal serum PlGF and sFlt‐1 in combination with maternal characteristics, fetal biometry and other serum markers (PAPP‐ A, free β‐hCG and AFP), in a model for prediction of delivery of SGA neonates at 19– 24 weeks, is not yet sufficiently accurate for clinical use.
there is a lack of evidence to support or refute the use of maternal serum biomarkers in combination with maternal and fetal factors in the prediction of SGA in the absence of PE.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prediction of SGA neonates in the absence of PE is not possible at this time.

maternal serum PlGF and sFlt‐1 concentrations at 19–20 weeks' gestation in combination with maternal characteristics and fetal biometry at 11–14 weeks' gestation are useful for the prediction of SGA at delivery, and may be of value in determining whether the third‐ trimester ultrasound scan should be performed.
maternal serum PlGF and PAPP‐A concentrations, in combination with the maternal factors and fetal biparietal diameter (BPD), are valuable in the prediction of SGA delivery in the absence of PE.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use a combination of maternal factors and maternal serum biomarkers to identify those pregnancies at risk for SGA delivery.
the use of maternal serum PlGF and sFlt‐1 in combination with fetal biometry and maternal factors at 19–21 weeks can be useful to identify women who are at risk for delivering a SGA infant.
the combination of maternal serum biomarkers with maternal factors and second‐trimester ultrasound measurements can be used to identify women with an increased risk for delivery of SGA neonates.
